# MCP

The app's MCP endpoint, through which a person's AI client lists resources, finds and reads records, and, when turned on, creates and updates them with that person's access and approval.

An app can serve an MCP endpoint: a person adds its address to an AI client that speaks MCP, such as a chat assistant or a code editor, signs in on the app and allows the client. The client then works with that person's access: it lists the resources and fields they may read, finds records with the API's filters, sorting and pages, and reads one record.

## Turning it on

`auth.mcp` in `protobase.config.ts` turns it on:

```ts
export default defineConfig({ auth: { mcp: true } })
```

Every auth store has the OAuth tables, so turning it on needs no migration. The endpoint is `https://<app>/api/mcp`, or the path `auth.mcp.path` names. How clients register, how people sign in and allow them, and how they disconnect them is in [OAuth for MCP clients](auth.md#oauth-for-mcp-clients).

## Connecting a client

Give the client the endpoint's address. It finds the app's sign-in from there, opens it in the browser, and the person signs in and allows it on the app's connect page.

- A chat assistant usually takes a remote MCP server, or custom connector, in its settings: add one with the address.
- A code editor or agent usually reads its MCP servers from a JSON file, in this shape or close to it:

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "my-app": { "url": "https://my-app.example.com/api/mcp" } } }
  ```

  Some take the address on the command line instead, as a server with the HTTP transport, and sign in when you first use it.

## The tools

Each tool reads as the signed-in person: their role's access rules, row filters, tenant and hidden fields apply as in the [REST API](api.md#access).

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `list_resources` | The resources the person may read, with their labels, key, whether they soft delete (`soft_delete`) and fields: each field's type, label, enum values, the resource a relation links to, and whether filters and sorts take it. |
| `list_records` | A page of a resource's records: `filter` in the API's [filter syntax](api.md#filters), `order_by`, `page_size` (20 by default, at most 100) and `page_token`, with `next_page_token` for the next page. `show_deleted: true` also returns soft-deleted records. |
| `get_record` | One record by its key, with its ETag. A composite key is passed as the values of its fields, in order. `show_deleted: true` also finds a soft-deleted record. |

`show_deleted` works as the [REST API](api.md#routes)'s: it applies only to a resource with a soft delete, and is refused on any other. Soft-deleted records come under the same access rules, tenant and hidden fields as the rest, and carry the field their deletion set.

A refusal, such as a resource the person may not read or a bad filter, comes back to the client as text it can act on, `{ "error": ..., "message": ... }`.

### SQL for admins

`mcpEndpoint.sql` also offers `run_read_only_query`, as in the [assistant](assistant.md#the-built-in-backend), to people with the `admin` or `ai` role:

```ts
export default defineConfig({ auth: { mcp: true }, mcpEndpoint: { sql: true } })
```

It runs one `SELECT` in a read-only transaction, as the app's database role, **outside the access rules and tenant scoping**: whoever has one of those roles reads the whole database through it. Give those roles only to people who may see all of the data.

### Writes

`mcpEndpoint.writes` also offers four tools that change records, to everyone signed in:

```ts
export default defineConfig({ auth: { mcp: true }, mcpEndpoint: { writes: true } })
```

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `create_record` | Creates a record of a resource from `data`, field names to values, and returns it with its ETag. |
| `update_record` | Changes the fields in `data` of one record by its key, and returns it with its new ETag. With the `etag` that `get_record` gave, it fails when someone changed the record since. It does not set the field a soft delete sets: a delete goes through `delete_record`. |
| `delete_record` | Deletes one record by its key and the `etag` that `get_record` gave, and fails when someone changed the record since. A resource with a [soft delete](data-config.md) keeps the record, deleted; any other loses it for good. |
| `batch_write` | Creates, updates and deletes records across resources in one transaction, see [Batch writes](#batch-writes). |

Each write goes through the REST API as the person: their role's access rules, `validate`, write hooks, events and webhooks apply, so the client can do only what the person may do in the app.

Before each write the client asks the person to approve it, through MCP's form elicitation. The approval names the record as the record page's breadcrumb does, by the resource's label, its key and its title, such as `Update Task #42 "Fix the sign-in lockout"?`. An update lists each field it changes by its label, with its value before and after (`Status: In flight -> Done`); a create lists the new record's fields by their labels; a delete says whether the record can be restored, and for a resource without a soft delete says plainly that it cannot be undone. Enum values show by their labels, a [sensitive](data-config.md#sensitive-fields) field's value is hidden, and a value is cut at 200 characters. A record or field the person may not read is named by its key or its name in words, and an update or delete of a record changed since its `etag` is refused before asking. The approval, its button and the refusal for a client that cannot ask are in the person's [language](languages.md): the app's `locale`, or else the one the client's request accepts (`Accept-Language`). Nothing is written until they approve, and declining writes nothing. A client's own setting that always allows a tool is not this approval. An approval holds only for the call it was asked for, with the same arguments, by the same person in the same app, organization and client, and only once, within 10 minutes; any other call is asked again. A client that cannot ask, one without form elicitation or one on the 2025 protocol, gets each write refused with a message saying so.

<gap>An approval cannot be answered on another server instance or after a restart because a shared approval store is not implemented.</gap> Behind a load balancer, send an MCP client's calls to the same instance.

To offer the writes on some resources only, list them:

```ts
mcpEndpoint: { writes: { resources: ['tasks'] } }
```

The write tools then name those resources in their descriptions, and refuse a write to any other before asking, with `{ "error": "forbidden", "message": ... }` saying which resources they write; nothing is written. A name the app has no resource for stops the server at startup. The list only narrows the writes: the person's access rules still apply on the listed resources.

#### Writes without approval

An app that runs service accounts over MCP, such as a backend job or an agent with no person present, names their roles in `mcpEndpoint.writes`:

```ts
mcpEndpoint: { writes: { resources: ['tasks'], rolesWithoutApproval: ['service'] } }
```

A user with one of those roles creates, updates and deletes records over MCP without the approval step: the client is never asked, so a client that cannot ask writes too. Their role's access rules and the listed resources still limit every write as before, so a job with no person present can keep the app's data over MCP and do nothing there it could not do through the REST API. Everyone else is still asked before each write. Taking the role away, banning or deleting the account stops its tokens at their next request, not when they expire.

No role is exempt unless named. The roles are checked against the signed-in user, not against the client, and a user holding several is exempt when any of them is named. A name that is not one of the app's roles, or is `anonymous`, stops the server at startup. Naming a role a person signs in with lets any client that person allows write as them unasked.

<gap>A deleted record cannot be restored over MCP.</gap> There is no SQL that writes.

#### Batch writes

`batch_write` takes a list of creates, updates and deletes, each naming its resource, with the key and ETag for an update or delete, and runs them in order in one transaction, as the REST API's [batch writes](api.md#batch-writes) do: either all of them are written or none, and a record changed since its ETag fails the whole batch.

```json
{ "operations": [
  { "op": "create", "resource": "tasks", "data": { "title": "Plan the release" }, "ref": "task" },
  { "op": "create", "resource": "task_links", "data": { "task_id": { "$ref": "task" }, "url": "https://example.com" } },
  { "op": "update", "resource": "tasks", "key": 12, "etag": "\"3\"", "data": { "status": "done" } },
  { "op": "delete", "resource": "task_links", "key": 40, "etag": "\"1\"" }
] }
```

An update needs the `etag` the record was read with, or `"*"` for any version; a delete's `etag` is optional, and without one it deletes any version. A create may name itself with `ref`, and a later operation's key or data value `{ "$ref": "<name>" }` is that record's key. The result is `{ "results": [...] }`, as the REST batch answers: each created or updated record with its new ETag, so the client can go on writing.

The person approves the batch once, seeing each write in it: how many creates, updates and deletes it makes on each resource, then each operation with its key and data, the first 50 in full and the rest counted. The approval says plainly when deletes in it cannot be undone, which is every delete on a resource that does not [soft delete](data-config.md#resource).

A batch is checked before the person is asked: an operation other than a create, update or delete, a field an operation does not take, an update without an ETag or more than 500 operations come back as `{ "error": "invalid-argument", "message": ... }` naming the operation, and with writes limited to some resources an operation on any other refuses the whole batch. An update does not set the field a soft delete sets, as `update_record` does not: a delete goes through a delete operation. A refusal while it runs, such as an operation the person may not do or a stale ETag, comes back with the REST batch's `operation` (its index), `op` and `resource`. Either way nothing is written.

## Browsers and hosts

A client in a browser may call the endpoint from any origin: it sends its token, never cookies. A request addressed to another host than that of the app's [`url`](config/app.md#url) is refused, against DNS rebinding.

The endpoint serves each request on its own, without an MCP session: a `GET` or `DELETE` answers 405.

## Building on it

`@protobase/server` exports the pieces the endpoint is made of, for an MCP server of your own with tools of your own:

- `mcpHandler({ authenticate, resource, scope, server })`: the endpoint as a fetch handler. It checks the host, admits a valid token (`mcpGate`) and serves the request with the server that `server(session, request)` builds for its caller; `request` is the HTTP request, such as for the language the person reads.
- `mcpServer({ info, tools, context, report, rolesWithoutApproval, approvals })`: an MCP server offering [assistant tools](assistant.md#the-apps-own-tools), each with its JSON Schema and its `annotations`, MCP's tool hints. `context` is the tools' context without `approve`, with the `locale` its approvals are asked in (English when absent): each call gets its own, which asks the client's user, or approves at once when the session's user holds one of `rolesWithoutApproval`. `approvals` is `mcpApprovals()`, built once and passed to every server the endpoint builds: it keeps the approvals asked for until they are answered or expire.
- `mcpTools({ db, sql, writes })`: the default tools for a session; `writes` is `true`, `false` or `{ resources, rolesWithoutApproval }`.
- `readRecordTools()`, or `listResourcesTool()`, `listRecordsTool()` and `getRecordTool()`: the read tools alone; `readOnlyQueryTool(db)` is `run_read_only_query`, and `readWriteQueryTool(db)` proposes one write statement that the user approves before it runs.
- `writeRecordTools({ resources })`, or `createRecordTool(...)`, `updateRecordTool(...)` and `deleteRecordTool(...)`: the single write tools alone, on the listed resources or, without `resources`, on any; `batchWriteTool({ resources })` is `batch_write` alone.
- `mcpGate({ authenticate, resource, scope })`: the token check alone, answering 401 or 403 with a challenge that names the resource's metadata.
- `mcpToolContext(...)`, `mcpRoutes(app, { path, handler })` and `sessionOf(authInfo)`: the tools' context as the app builds it, the routes with open CORS, and the session a request was admitted with.

A host that builds its own server around `createAdmin`, rather than running the project with `protobase dev` or `protobase serve`, can serve its own endpoint at `auth.mcp.path` instead: `mcpEndpoint: false` (`createAdmin`'s `options.mcp`) turns Protobase's off, and the host mounts its own in front of `createAdmin`'s app. The OAuth provider and its discovery stay, and `createAdmin` answers 404 at the path and under it. `protobase dev` and `protobase serve` have no place to mount another endpoint, so in a project served by them `mcpEndpoint: false` only turns the endpoint off.

A tool of your own goes on the server `server` returns, with the context its tools get. `authenticate` is the host's own `Authenticator`: it verifies the client's access token for the endpoint's address, its audience, and returns a session with the `client` the token was issued to:

```ts
import { defineTool, mcpApprovals, mcpHandler, mcpServer, type Session, type ToolContext } from '@protobase/server'

const ping = defineTool({
  name: 'ping',
  description: 'Answers pong.',
  parameters: { type: 'object', properties: {} },
  annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
  run: async () => 'pong',
})

const context = (session: Session): Omit<ToolContext, 'approve'> => ({
  session,
  records: myRecords(session),
  resources: async () => ({ models: [], views: [] }),
  show: () => {},
})

const approvals = mcpApprovals()

const handler = mcpHandler({
  authenticate: verifyMcpToken,
  resource: 'https://admin.example.com/api/mcp',
  scope: 'mcp',
  server: (session) => mcpServer({ info: { name: 'My app', version: '1.0.0' }, tools: [ping], context: context(session), report: console.error, approvals }),
})
```

A tool that changes something calls `context.approve(...)` before it changes anything, and only once: over MCP the client asks the person, then calls the tool again from the start with their answer, and `approve` then resolves with it.

`mcpServer` returns the SDK's `McpServer`, so `registerTool` on it adds a tool written against the SDK directly.
